# What a modeller does during an outbreak

## The loop

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
- Counts arrive by report date. The infections happened days or weeks
  earlier
- Estimate the delays first, then unpick them from the counts to get
  infections and $R_t$
- A renewal process: today's infections are $R_t$ times a weighted sum
  of recent infections, weighted by the generation interval. Run it
  backwards to estimate, forwards to forecast
- Someone decides. Then next week's data arrive
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](../figures/keynote-loop.png){width="100%"
fig-alt="Four teal boxes in a row, data arrive, delays, infections and
Rt, forecasts and scenarios, joined by arrows, with a red box labelled a
decision below and a red return arrow labelled new data, next week
running back to the first box."}

::: {.attribution}
Diagram this talk, `scripts/keynote-schematics.py`, after
[A workflow for infectious disease modelling][wf], Abbott et al.
:::
:::

## A renewal process, by hand

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
- $I_t = R_t \sum_s I_{t-s}\, g_s$
- $g_s$ is the generation interval (GI), the delay from one infection
  to the next
- Above one, growth. Below one, decline. The generation interval sets
  how fast
- Move the sliders
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof R = Inputs.range([0.5, 2.0], {
  value: 1.3, step: 0.05, label: "R"
})
viewof gmean = Inputs.range([2, 12], {
  value: 5, step: 0.5, label: "Mean GI, days"
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
renewal = {
  const days = 60, k = 4, theta = gmean / k;
  const g = Array.from({length: 24}, (_, i) => {
    const s = i + 1;
    return Math.pow(s, k - 1) * Math.exp(-s / theta);
  });
  const gsum = g.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
  const gn = g.map((v) => v / gsum);
  const inf = new Array(days).fill(0);
  for (let t = 0; t < 5; t++) inf[t] = 10;
  for (let t = 5; t < days; t++) {
    let s = 0;
    for (let j = 0; j < gn.length && t - 1 - j >= 0; j++) {
      s += inf[t - 1 - j] * gn[j];
    }
    inf[t] = R * s;
  }
  return inf.map((y, t) => ({day: t, infections: y}));
}
Plot.plot({
  width: 1000,
  height: 460,
  marginLeft: 70,
  style: {fontSize: "18px"},
  y: {type: "log", label: "Infections per day", grid: true},
  x: {label: "Day"},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([10], {stroke: "#8a8f98", strokeDasharray: "4 4"}),
    Plot.line(renewal, {
      x: "day", y: "infections", stroke: "#1f6f8b", strokeWidth: 3.5
    })
  ]
})
```

::: {.attribution}
Constant $R$, a gamma-shaped generation interval with shape 4, ten
infections a day seeded for five days. Interactive this talk.
:::
:::

## What keeps going wrong

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
- Delays estimated during growth are too short. The long ones have not
  happened yet
- Chained models pass on a point estimate. The interval at the end is
  too narrow
- Bespoke code for each outbreak. Slow to adapt when the data change
- "We sometimes published nonsensical estimates"

::: {.callout-note}
Half of the 105 Belgian COVID-19 models reviewed by Bagaforo et al.
2026 had no behaviour component.
:::
